clue.text: Sheep and lambs going astray — curses!

indicators.note: animals going astray wander off in all directions, so the letters of the two words are scattered and regathered

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A shepherd swears as the flock and its young wander off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going astray' rearranges SHEEP and LAMBS together; 'and' just joins them.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are plural nouns for profane oaths or impious utterances.

clue.text: Visit a joint, receiving the go-ahead

indicators.note: the joint is receiving the approval word, which goes inside it

parts.note: loin is a joint of meat
OK is approval, the go-ahead

explanation.surface: A visit to a nightspot is given clearance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'joint' suggests a disreputable venue, but it is a cut of meat.
explanation.definitionFit: To drop by briefly is to pay a short call.

clue.text: Language used in most outlandish area of Britain

indicators.note: the language is used in the rearranged letters, placed inside them
outlandish means bizarre, so the letters of the next word are put in a strange order

parts.note: Erse is the Gaelic language of Scotland or Ireland

explanation.surface: A strange local dialect is spoken in a far-flung corner of Britain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outlandish' scrambles the word most, and 'used in' places the old Gaelic tongue inside. Somerset is a county in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: This English county in the West Country is a region of the island of Great Britain.

clue.text: Be extremely obstructive, bringing up the rear

definitions.meaning: get in the way as much as possible

explanation.definitionFit: The word splits as a phrase meaning obstruct to the greatest degree, and as a whole it means rearmost.

clue.text: A Roman writer full of fighting spirit

definitions.meaning: A Latin poet famous for his epigrams

explanation.definitionFit: The epigrammatist shares his name with an adjective meaning warlike, from Mars, god of war.

clue.text: Fizzy drink giving rise to difficulties?

indicators.note: in a down clue giving rise means the word is written upwards, bottom to top

parts.note: ados are fusses or troubles

explanation.surface: A carbonated beverage is blamed for causing problems.
explanation.walkthrough: 'giving rise to' reads as causing, but in a down clue it turns ADOS upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Soda water is a carbonated, bubbly beverage.

clue.text: Blunt criticism of builder joining club

indicators.note: joining puts one piece right next to the other

parts.note: a brick is the builder's basic block
a bat is a club, as in cricket or baseball

explanation.surface: A tradesman becoming a member of a club meets harsh comments.
explanation.walkthrough: A brickbat was literally a piece of brick thrown as a missile, hence harsh criticism.
explanation.definitionFit: A brickbat is a cutting remark, a verbal missile aimed at someone.

clue.text: Offers fantastic reductions

indicators.note: fantastic suggests something wildly fanciful, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A shop advertises its amazing sale prices.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Offers' looks like a noun for bargains, but it is the verb: presents.
explanation.definitionFit: To present or bring forward something new is to put it forward.

clue.text: Decoration one king's bestowed on another

parts.note: the OBE (Order of the British Empire) is a British honour
R stands for rex, Latin for king
taken as written

explanation.surface: A monarch confers an honour on a fellow sovereign.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition 'another' means another king: Oberon is king of the fairies in A Midsummer Night's Dream. 'bestowed' is surface padding linking the pieces; the OBE is an honour given by the British monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's fairy monarch is a second royal figure alongside the king named in the wordplay.

clue.text: It's not so unusual to see monarch on public land

indicators.note: in an across clue, one piece on another means it comes after it

parts.note: a common is open land shared by a community
ER, Elizabeth Regina, the Queen

explanation.surface: Spotting the sovereign on the village green is no rare event.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's not so unusual' is a comparative: more common. A COMMON is shared open land in a British village or town.
explanation.definitionFit: The comparative of an adjective meaning ordinary or frequent describes something less rare.

clue.text: He denounces dealer holding copper back

indicators.note: the dealer word is holding something, so the other piece sits inside it

parts.note: a trader is someone who deals in goods

indicators.note: back means the symbol for copper is read the other way round

parts.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper

explanation.surface: An informer accuses a merchant of keeping stolen copper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns the chemical symbol round, and 'holding' places it inside the dealer word; 'He denounces' is a noun definition, one who denounces.
explanation.definitionFit: A slanderer or defamer is one who speaks ill of others, i.e. denounces them.

clue.text: Social workers some can't stomach

indicators.note: some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Some people cannot bear those who work in social services.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Social workers' suggests care staff, but insects in a colony are meant.
explanation.definitionFit: These insects live in organised colonies where workers share labour, a classic crossword image.

clue.text: Scientist who finds his work heavenly

definitions.text: Scientist who finds his work heavenly

parts.words: Scientist who finds his work heavenly
parts.note: reads as a researcher who loves his job, but means one whose field of study is the heavens

explanation.surface: A researcher who adores what he does.
explanation.definitionFit: This scientist studies stars and planets, the celestial bodies of the sky.

clue.text: Taken in — not for the first time!

definitions.text: Taken in — not for the first time!

parts.words: Taken in — not for the first time!
parts.note: reads like being fooled once again, but means soaked up or absorbed a second time

explanation.surface: Someone laments being deceived yet again.
explanation.definitionFit: Absorbed again: taken in, as by a sponge, on a repeated occasion.

clue.text: The instant assessment is "Could do better"

parts.note: a second is an instant, a moment
a rate is an assessment or valuation

explanation.surface: A teacher's snap verdict on a report card says room to improve.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Could do better' is the classic school-report comment, standing here for mediocre.
explanation.definitionFit: Something mediocre or inferior falls short of the best and leaves room for improvement.

clue.text: Out, in, out — it is good training

indicators.note: out, as in out of order or out of place, says the preceding words are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A coach's drill of stepping out and in is praised as fine practice.
explanation.walkthrough: The second 'out' is the anagram signal for OUT, IN and IT; 'is' links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Instruction or teaching given to pupils is a form of schooling or coaching.

clue.text: No practical individual is thought to enter

parts.note: an idea is a thought
to list is to enter, as in a register or catalogue

explanation.surface: A dreamer is the sort to join in with notions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is' links the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A dreamer who pursues lofty principles rather than realistic aims is unpragmatic.

clue.text: Person who scoffs mushroom, retained in stomach mostly

indicators.note: the mushroom is retained in the shortened word, placed inside it
mostly means the word is cut short by its final letter

parts.note: to stick something is to tolerate or stomach it
the cep is an edible mushroom, the porcino

explanation.surface: Someone eats a mushroom and keeps it down, more or less.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scoffs' suggests eating greedily, as the mushroom picture invites, but it means mocks. 'mostly' drops the final letter of the word for stomach before the mushroom goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A doubter who mocks claims they don't believe is a scoffer.

clue.text: I'll stick around -that's sweet

indicators.note: the glue word goes around the other piece

parts.note: to paste is to stick with glue
the letters of the word with its apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: Someone promises to stay nearby, and is thanked for kindness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sweet' looks like an exclamation of approval but names a confection.
explanation.definitionFit: A pastille is a small lozenge or chewy confection.

clue.text: Employee on strike issued statement

parts.note: a hand is a worker, as in a farm hand
out means on strike, as in the workers are out

explanation.surface: A striking worker releases a press release.
explanation.definitionFit: A handout is a printed release given out to the press or public.

clue.text: Work extra hard on account of the family

parts.note: over can mean about or on account of, as in a quarrel over money
a strain is a line of descent or lineage

explanation.surface: Someone toils too much for the sake of their relatives.
explanation.definitionFit: To push oneself beyond healthy limits is to overexert.

clue.text: From what we hear, appropriate main parts

indicators.note: from what we hear says the word for appropriate is spoken, giving a word that sounds the same

parts.note: to appropriate is to take possession of, to seize

explanation.surface: Rumour says someone is taking over the key sections.
explanation.walkthrough: 'main' reads as chief but is the old poetic word for the open ocean.
explanation.definitionFit: The main is the open ocean, so parts of it are bodies of salt water.

clue.text: A link without a French connection

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the first pieces surround the French article

parts.note: a tie is a link or bond
un is French for a

explanation.surface: A bond with no French connection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' means outside, not lacking. 'connection' is a relative, as in family connections.
explanation.definitionFit: A connection can mean a relative, and an aunt is a family relation.

clue.text: Well-equipped fuel supplier

parts.note: reads as a well-stocked fuel merchant, but means a supplier of fuel equipped with wells

explanation.surface: A fuel merchant with all the right gear.
explanation.definitionFit: A tract with drilled wells produces petroleum, a fuel, so it supplies fuel via its wells.

clue.text: So. with some hesitation, proceed

parts.note: er is a hesitant sound
to go is to proceed

explanation.surface: Someone hesitantly announces it is time to move on.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin for therefore, used to introduce a conclusion.

clue.text: None sleep too long without incurring trouble

parts.note: nought, zero, written O
a nap is a short sleep
late means overdue, having taken too long

explanation.surface: No one sleeps in and gets into difficulty.
explanation.definitionFit: Handed something on a plate means getting it effortlessly, with no struggle at all.

clue.text: For example, accepting sloth, say, can be relaxing

indicators.note: the abbreviation is accepting the other piece, holding it inside

parts.note: e.g. is short for exempli gratia, for example
sloth is one of the seven deadly sins, so it is an example of a sin

explanation.surface: Tolerating a little laziness can help one unwind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sloth' looks like the animal, but it is a deadly sin; 'can be' links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Loosening or slackening off tension is a gerund-like synonym of letting up.

clue.text: Not inclined to be sincere

definitions.meaning: honest and above board, the idiom meaning genuine

explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means both flat with no slope and honest or straight-dealing.
